headline: 71.2°F on the Bight Buoy — the Hudson's Warm-Water Regime Isn't Cracking Yet
subhead: A steady southerly swell and a stubborn warm eddy are keeping yellowfin, bigeye, and mahi stacked along the canyon edges, but the bite is a puzzle you have to work, not a gimme.
body_markdown:
Seventy-one point two degrees. That's the read off Buoy 44025 out in the Bight this week, riding on top of a 3.9-foot swell out of the south at a soft 5-second period. It's not a dramatic number by itself, but it tells the story of a surface layer that's stayed warm and stable all the way out to the shelf break, and that matters because the same warm eddy that's carried the Hudson all August still hasn't been pushed off. No front has come through strong enough to flip the water, and the southwest 8-to-12-knot wind pattern that's held for days now isn't the kind that stirs things up — it's the kind that lets blue water sit and settle in against the canyon wall.

That stability is exactly why the mixed bag has held together out here. Yellowfin, some bigeye, mahi, and white marlin have all been coming out of the same general water, which tells you the canyon's structure is doing its job — pushing bait up out of deep water and letting predators work it along a clean edge rather than a blown-out one. Squid showing up thick in the bait column is the tell. When squid stack in the water column over the canyon rim, tuna don't have to move far to eat, and that's been the pattern for a couple weeks running.

The better boats have been splitting time between the troll and the jig. Naked ballyhoo behind small green machines and cedar plugs is still the bread-and-butter spread for yellowfin working the 100-fathom line, especially where it bends around the eastern lip of the Claw. When the fish are sitting on bait rather than chasing the surface, that's when the vertical jig program takes over — butterfly-style jigs worked with a fast, erratic stroke down through 150 to 250 feet has been drawing strikes when the troll goes quiet, particularly over structure near the Dip where the bottom breaks sharp and bait gets funneled against the wall.

Mahi have been scattered but present anywhere there's a defined temp line or floating debris — weed clumps, lobster gear, the occasional pallet — holding just under the surface. A small skirted ballyhoo or a bare hook with a strip of squid drifted back near the transom while the spread is out has been picking off a few extra fish for boats willing to slow down and look. White marlin have shown on the troll in the same general water as the yellowfin, which is normal for this time of year when bait is dense and mixed species are working the same edge rather than separating by depth.

Bigeye have been a nighttime story more than a daytime one. Chunking butterfish on the drift after dark, fishing baits at staggered depths off the current, has produced fish in the same zone where the daytime troll bite has been happening — not a coincidence, since bigeye tend to sit deeper during daylight and rise with the bait column after dark. For boats running the deep-drop program for swordfish, the pattern hasn't changed much: baits fished on the bottom in the 1,200-to-1,600-foot range, squid strips with a glow stick or LED strobe near the hook, worked slow-and-steady drifts across structure near the Claw and the Dip where the bottom holds current-swept troughs. That's a grind more than a sure thing right now, and boats should treat it that way — a few fish a trip, not a pile.

Honest read on the week: this has been a solid, working bite, not a blowtorch. Some days the troll connects early and stays hot through the morning; other days boats have had to hunt, working the edges with the jig before finding fish stacked tighter than expected. The squid-driven bait base is keeping things interesting, but it's not evenly spread across the whole canyon, and boats that ran without checking the chlorophyll break before committing to a spot came home with a lighter fish count than the ones who worked the edge first.

Looking at the next 24 to 48 hours, expect more of the same — stable high pressure, that same light southwest wind, and no real push to move the warm-water regime off the canyon. That's good news for consistency; the pattern that's produced this week should hold through the weekend. The moon building toward full over the next two days will tighten up the tidal swings, and that usually sharpens the bite windows right at first light and again in the evening, when current movement against the canyon wall pulls bait up onto the structure hardest. By 72 hours out, the warm-water setup should still be intact, keeping the tuna and billfish bite going in the Mid-Atlantic canyons generally, Hudson included. The one thing worth watching is any hint of a cooler push working down from the north — nothing in the current pattern suggests it's close, but late August is exactly when that kind of shift starts to show up on the charts without much warning.

If there's only one day to make the run this week, the early window on the building tide — working the 100-fathom edge first, then sliding over toward the Claw or the Dip if the troll goes quiet — is the smart play. Keep the jig rigged and ready. When this bait-rich, stable pattern holds, the fish are there; the job is putting the spread or the jig in the right piece of water at the right hour, not hoping the whole ocean lights up at once.
